question: How do you test a pawn or piece that looks free in the Queen's Gambit Declined, and how do you see the tactic in the opponent's quiet move?
outcomes: Says what makes the grab on d5 fail in the Elephant Trap (an in-between check on an open diagonal, the queen taken with check, the king retaking) and checks those conditions before grabbing
Names the condition that makes the check fail (a pawn that attacks the checking square) and tells the working and the failing position apart
Explains the pin of the knight on c3 in the Cambridge Springs, why the knight on d2 must stay, and why retreating it to f3 loses a piece
Sees that a quiet knight jump can attack one piece and uncover a second attack (the bishop on e7 and the queen behind it) and answers it by trading or supporting
Spots a pawn fork before a retreat (the pawn push to e4 against a bishop on d3 and a knight on f3) and chooses a square that avoids it
Quotes our own counts (archive and masters) with their sample sizes and says what they do not show

content/items/lesson-od-l-od-qgd-6.json: every position is replayed move by move with python-chess from the stated moves; the a3 position and the Black-to-move copy are one-feature edits made for contrasts and are labelled as such in the position records [V]

Archive counts [V, this session]: Lichess broadcast database (CC0), monthly files January 2024 to September 2026 in library/data/games/lichess-broadcast, scanned as text for games beginning 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 (29,769 games, of which 1,064 have both players rated 2500 or more); 73 games reach the position after 5...exd5 in the 4.Bg5 Nbd7 move order; 13 of those continue 6.Nxd5 (White 1 win, 3 draws, 9 losses); 46 games reach 6...Qa5 in the Cambridge Springs move order. Ratings are as listed by the broadcast and are missing for some players

app/public/masters/stats.json (329,379 games, both players 2500+, first 24 plies, built 2026-10-29): counts quoted exactly from the tree rows keyed by position: 61 games at the hook position (only 6.e3 listed, a move is kept at 3 or more games); 291 games after 6...Qa5 (white 99, draw 134, black 58), of which 7.Nd2 143 (40/72/31) and 7.cxd5 137 (55/58/24) [V]
[R] The names Elephant Trap and Cambridge Springs are recalled, not re-checked in a source read here; the lines themselves are verified by replay and by the engine [R]

steps.caption: White to move after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5. The pawn on d5 is attacked once, by the knight on c3, and guarded once, by the knight on f6. That knight also seems tied to the queen on d8 by the bishop on g5. Would you take the pawn with the knight? Decide first, then read on.

claims.statement: One white piece attacks the pawn on d5 (the knight on c3).
One black piece guards the pawn on d5 (the knight on f6).
The bishop on g5 attacks the knight on f6.
The black queen stands on d8, behind the knight on f6 along the bishop line.

steps.prompt: Before any explanation, a quick guess. Would you play the knight to d5 here? If Black takes it with the knight from f6, what do you expect White to do next? One line each; you will come back to these answers at the end.

fields.label: My move for White and why:
What I expect after Black recaptures:

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** Some opening traps are bait: a pawn or piece that looks free. How do you test the bait before you bite, and see the same idea from the other side? By the end you can say why the grab on d5 fails, find the pin of the Cambridge Springs queen, spot a quiet knight jump that hits two pieces, and see a pawn fork before a retreat. Every claim about a result is engine-checked at depth 16.

steps.caption: Step through the grab. Watch the seventh move: it is not a recapture.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn. White hopes the knight on f6 is stuck, pinned against the queen.
Black recaptures anyway. The knight leaves f6 and the bishop on g5 now attacks the queen.
White takes the queen.
Black does not retake. The bishop checks along a diagonal that the d-pawn and the knight have left open.
White has to meet the check, and the queen steps in.
The bishop takes the queen, again with check.
The king takes the bishop.
The king takes the bishop. White is now a knight down for a pawn.

claims.statement: After the knight recaptures on d5, the bishop on g5 attacks the queen on d8.
The bishop on b4 gives check to the king on e1.
The black king ends on d8.
The white king ends on d2, after its queen and bishop are gone.
At depth 16 the engine puts White well behind: the evaluation (White's view) is between -560 and -350 centipawns.

steps.caption: Black to move after the queen was taken. What if Black simply retakes? Step through the plain recapture.

line.say: The tempting recapture. White has won a queen and a pawn for a knight and a bishop.

claims.statement: The black king stands on d8 after the recapture.
At depth 16 the plain recapture leaves White well ahead: between 450 and 660 centipawns (White's view).

steps.text: **Why the check works.** It is an *in-between move*: a forcing check before the recapture. Four things hold together. The bishop has a clear path to b4. The line from b4 to the king is open, because the knight and the d-pawn have left it. The only answer, the queen stepping in, is taken with check. And the king can retake on d8. Remove one and the trap fails.

steps.title: Does the in-between check help?
steps.prompt: Predict first. In both positions White has just taken the queen with the bishop on d8 and it is Black's move. They differ in one thing only: the first has White's a-pawn on a2, the second has it on a3. Can Black win material back with a check on b4?

steps.caption: What White plays instead. Step through the calm move.

line.say: White solves the question by not grabbing: e3 supports the pawn on d4 and frees the bishop on f1.
Black develops the bishop and unpins the queen from the bishop on g5.
The bishop aims at the kingside; White has a small, calm advantage.
Black castles. No pawn was grabbed and no one is in a hurry.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the quiet moves e3, Nf3 and Qc2 are all within 0.4 pawns of the best (e3 is the top choice).
After the quiet line the engine gives White a small edge: between -40 and 110 centipawns (White's view).

steps.caption: Black to move after 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.e3 c6 6.Nf3. This is the Cambridge Springs set-up (named after a tournament; the name is recalled, not re-checked here). [R] Step through Black's idea.

line.say: The queen attacks the knight on c3. The white king stands behind it on the same diagonal.

claims.statement: The queen on a5 attacks the knight on c3.
The white king stands on e1, on the same diagonal behind the knight.
One black piece attacks the knight on c3 (the queen).

steps.caption: White to move after 6...Qa5. Try to find a legal move for the knight on c3 (the claim below says there is none). Then step through the usual answer.

line.say: White's usual answer: the knight blocks on d2, between the knight on c3 and the king.
Black adds a second attacker: the bishop on b4 attacks c3, and the queen stands behind it.
White adds a defender of c3 and steps off the first rank.
Black castles. The knight on d2 now has a job: if it leaves, the pin comes back.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 has no legal move: it is pinned to the king.
The knight cannot capture on d5.
After ...Bb4 the bishop attacks the knight on c3.
The queen on a5 defends the bishop on b4.
The white knight stands on d2, between c3 and the king on e1.

steps.text: **The pin and its price.** A pinned piece is frozen, not lost. You can block the line, chase the pinning piece or give the king room. Each cure has a price: here the blocker on d2 is tied, and if it moves the pin returns. Before you move a blocker, count what attacks the piece behind it.

steps.caption: White to move after 7.Nd2 Bb4. One natural move loses at once. Step through it and count the attackers of the knight on c3.

line.say: The knight steps back to f3, a natural square, and uncovers the line to the king.
The knight jump attacks c3 and g5. The knight on c3 is pinned again, so it cannot take on e4.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the knight retreat loses at least a knight's worth compared with the best move.
The knight on e4 attacks both the knight on c3 and the bishop on g5.
Two black pieces attack the knight on c3 directly (the bishop and the knight); the queen stands behind the bishop, so three count in the exchange.
One white piece guards the knight on c3 (the pawn on b2).
After the jump the engine puts Black clearly ahead: the evaluation (White's view) is between -470 and -260 centipawns.

steps.title: Does the knight jump win a piece?
steps.prompt: Predict first. Both positions come from the Cambridge Springs set-up. In the first the white knight has just stepped back from d2 to f3. In the second it is still on d2, and it is Black's move. Does ...Ne4 win a piece?

steps.caption: White to move after 6...Qa5. The jump does not always work: here White has an in-between move of his own. Black's best reply to it is to take on e6; the other black tries lose more.

line.say: White takes a pawn, and for the moment is a pawn up.
The knight jump again: it attacks the bishop on g5, and the knight on c3 is pinned.
An in-between capture: the pawn takes on e6, and Black must recapture before the jump pays off.
Black recaptures; this is the engine's choice, and White still has the bishop on g5 to look after.
The bishop steps back with the pin on the knight on f6 gone, and White keeps a clear edge.

claims.statement: After the in-between capture, the recapture and the bishop's retreat the engine gives White a clear edge: between -20 and 190 centipawns (White's view).
A white pawn stands on e6 after the capture.

steps.caption: Black to move in the Orthodox Defence, after 8.Bd3 dxc4 9.Bxc4. Step through the quiet jump to d5 and count what it attacks.

line.say: The knight jumps to d5. It attacks c3 and opens the bishop's line to g5: two pieces are attacked.
White takes first: trading the attacked bishop removes one of the two threats.
The queen retakes.
White castles. The knight on c3 stays guarded by the rook and the b-pawn.
Black trades the knights.
The rook retakes.
Black strikes at the centre. The position is level.

claims.statement: The knight on d5 attacks the knight on c3.
After the jump one black piece attacks the bishop on g5 (the bishop on e7).
One white piece guards the bishop on g5 (the knight on f3).
At depth 16 the final position is close to level: between -40 and 110 centipawns (White's view).

steps.chapter: A quiet move that hits two pieces

steps.caption: White to move after 9...Nd5. Step through what happens if White ignores the attack on the bishop.

line.say: A natural developing move that ignores the attack on the bishop.
Black takes the bishop.
White retakes with the knight, which now stands on g5.
The queen was behind the bishop on the same diagonal, so the knight on g5 has no protection left.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the move Qc2 loses at least a piece compared with the best move.
A black queen stands on g5 at the end.
The engine puts Black clearly ahead: between -690 and -480 centipawns (White's view).

steps.text: **Count the line behind.** A piece is attacked by what sees it and by what is lined up behind that. The bishop on e7 attacked g5 once, with the queen behind it on the same diagonal: two attackers against one defender, though the board showed one. The jump did two jobs at once: it attacked, and it uncovered. Against a quiet move, ask what it uncovered.

steps.title: Does Qc2 lose a piece?
steps.prompt: Predict first. In both positions Black's knight has just jumped to d5 and it is White's move. They differ in one thing only: the black queen stands on d8 in the first and on e8 in the second. Does the quiet move Qc2 lose a piece?

steps.caption: White to move in the same Orthodox line, after 12...e5. The bishop on c4 wants a better square. Step through the most natural retreat.

line.say: The bishop retreats to d3, where it eyes the kingside. The retreat looks natural.
The pawn attacks the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 at once. The queen guards the pawn.
The bishop moves out of the way; the knight on f3 is still attacked.
The pawn takes the knight.
White retakes and is a knight down for a pawn.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the retreat Bd3 loses at least a piece compared with the best move.
After ...e4 the pawn attacks both d3 and f3.
One black piece guards the pawn on e4 (the queen).
One white piece attacks the pawn on e4 (the bishop).
The engine puts Black clearly ahead at the end: between -560 and -350 centipawns (White's view).

steps.chapter: A retreat into a pawn fork

steps.text: **When a pawn fork works.** Two valuable pieces stand on the two squares a pawn attacks from one step ahead. The square in front of the pawn is empty. The pawn is guarded, or taking it costs more than it wins. And you have no in-between answer, such as a check. Before a retreat, ask which enemy pawn could advance and attack this square, and what else stands beside it.

steps.title: Does ...e4 win a piece?
steps.prompt: Predict first. In both positions Black has played ...e5 and White has retreated the bishop from c4, and it is Black's move. In the first the bishop went to d3; in the second it went to b3. The pawn push ...e4 is possible in both. Does it win a piece?

steps.caption: The safe version. Step through the retreat to b3 and the same pawn push.

line.say: The bishop keeps its diagonal and stays off the fork squares.
Black plays the push anyway; it attacks the knight on f3 and nothing else.
The knight steps away to d2. The pawn on e4 has gained space, no more.

claims.statement: The pawn on e4 attacks the knight on f3.
The white knight stands on d2 at the end.
At depth 16 the position is about level: between -40 and 130 centipawns (White's view).

steps.text: **How often is the bait taken?** [V] Our archive: 29,769 broadcast games (January 2024 to September 2026) begin with the Queen's Gambit Declined. In 73 the hook position arose, and White grabbed the pawn in 13: one win, three draws, nine losses for the grabber. The top listed rating was 1926. [V] Our masters data (both sides 2500+, 329,379 games): 61 games reach it, and the only move listed with three or more games is the calm one.

**How often is the pin played?** [V] Our masters data (move orders merged): after the queen came to a5, 291 games; White scored 57% (99 wins, 134 draws, 58 losses). White blocked on d2 in 143 (53%) and took on d5 in 137 (61%). In our archive (all strengths) the position arose in 46 games. [I] The sample shows the pin is played at the top, not which side is better.

steps.prompt: The grab on d5 appears 13 times in our broadcast games, all with players rated below 2000, and not once with players rated 2500 or more. [H] Two explanations: strong players know the trap, or strong players rarely reach the position. How could you tell the two apart with games of your own? Write one test.

fields.label: A test that separates the two explanations:

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a friend who knows how the pieces move. Write five sentences: (1) why the grab on d5 fails, (2) what the in-between check needs, (3) what the knight on d2 is for in the Cambridge Springs and what happens if it leaves, (4) what the jump to d5 does to the bishop on g5, (5) the question you ask before retreating a piece. [H] Explaining a move to someone else tests whether you know its purpose.

fields.label: 1. Why the grab on d5 fails:

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say what had to be true (the clear diagonal, the pin, the line behind the bishop, the pawn's two target squares) rather than only naming the trap? Did you say what made each look-alike fail? Did you give one position someone could set up on a board? Did you name one question to ask before a capture or a retreat?

steps.prompt: Did your teach-back pass the self-check? Which of the five sentences was the weakest, and what would you add?

fields.label: The weakest sentence and what I would add:

steps.text: **What to remember.** A trap is a pattern with conditions, not a name. Before a capture, count the guards and ask what it uncovers and whether a check or capture can come in between. Before moving a blocker, count what attacks the piece behind it. After a quiet move, ask what it uncovered. Before a retreat, ask which pawn could advance onto an attack.

steps.prompt: Go back to your first answer about the knight on d5. Rewrite it in a better sentence: your move for White, and what has to be true for it to work.
